questions.question: What is a set in Python, and when is it useful?
questions.title: Python Set Basics
questions.direct_answer: A Python set is a mutable, unordered collection of distinct hashable elements. It is useful when uniqueness, average O(1) membership checks, or mathematical set operations matter, but it discards duplicate counts and should not be used when positional or insertion-order output is required.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you recognize uniqueness and repeated membership as set-shaped requirements without discarding needed order or counts.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Writing `{}` for an empty set or converting to a set when duplicate frequency and first-seen order matter.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use a `seen` set for one-pass duplicate detection and name `Counter` when occurrence counts are the real output.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: A set stores each distinct hashable value at most once.
Membership checks are average O(1), compared with O(n) scanning for a list.
Use `set()` for an empty set because `{}` creates an empty dictionary.
Sets are ideal for deduplication, seen-value tracking, and set relationships.
Do not rely on set iteration order, and remember that conversion loses duplicate counts.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A Python set is a mutable collection of distinct hashable values. Adding a value already present does not create a second copy, and a set provides no numeric indexes or sequence-order contract. Use `set()` for an empty set because `{}` creates an empty dictionary.

Sets use hash-based lookup, so `value in seen` is average `O(1)` instead of the average linear scan required by a list. Elements must be hashable: strings, numbers, and fully hashable tuples work, while lists and dictionaries do not. Collisions mean constant time is an average behavior rather than an unconditional promise.

A duplicate detector can keep a `seen` set while reading values once. If the next value is already present, it is a repeat; otherwise it is added for later checks. A separate output list can preserve the order in which duplicates are first discovered, while another set prevents the same duplicate from being reported repeatedly.

Converting `['a', 'b', 'a']` to a set keeps only `'a'` and `'b'`. It discards duplicate counts and should not be used when first-seen output order is required. Use `collections.Counter` when frequency is the result, and use `dict.fromkeys(values)` or a set-plus-list pattern when order must be preserved.

Choose a set when the real question is whether a value has been seen, which values overlap, or whether one group contains another. Keep a list when positions, duplicates, or iteration order are data, and use a dictionary when each key has an associated value. The example detects repeats without relying on the set's display order.

support.title: Detect duplicates in first-repeat order
support.code:
values = ["a", "b", "a", "c", "b", "a"]
seen = set()
reported = set()
duplicates = []

for value in values:
    if value in seen and value not in reported:
        duplicates.append(value)
        reported.add(value)
    seen.add(value)

print(sorted(seen))
print(duplicates)
support.caption: The sets provide membership, while the list preserves the order in which repeated values are first discovered.

beats.recallRule: Use a set for distinct hashable membership only when losing positions and duplicate counts is acceptable.

sections.title: A set changes the question from position to membership
sections.content:
A sequence answers “what is at position i?” A set answers “is this value present?” Its table uses hashes similarly to dictionary keys, which is why mutable containers cannot be elements. The data structure removes duplicate identity from the model instead of merely hiding duplicates in the display.

This makes a set powerful for validation and joins between small in-memory groups. It can also be the wrong choice: if the number of occurrences is important, use `Counter`; if first-seen order must be retained, combine a set for membership with a list for output or use `dict.fromkeys` for hashable values.

sections.title: One-pass duplicate detection
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  V[Read next value] --> Q{Value in seen?}
  Q -- Yes --> D[Report duplicate]
  Q -- No --> A[Add to seen]
  A --> V
```

sections.title: Find duplicates while preserving discovery order
sections.content:
```python
values = ["a", "b", "a", "c", "b"]
seen = set()
duplicates = []

for value in values:
    if value in seen and value not in duplicates:
        duplicates.append(value)
    seen.add(value)

print(seen)        # {'a', 'b', 'c'} in an unspecified display order
print(duplicates)  # ['a', 'b']
```

questions.question: How do union, intersection, difference, and symmetric difference work on Python sets?
questions.title: Python Set Operations
questions.direct_answer: Union keeps values from either set, intersection keeps values common to both, difference keeps values in the left set but not the right, and symmetric difference keeps values in exactly one set. Python writes these as `|`, `&`, `-`, and `^` respectively.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can translate a business relationship into union, intersection, directional difference, or symmetric difference.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating `a - b` as symmetric or confusing union with symmetric difference.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Express boolean relationships with subset and disjoint checks instead of building an unnecessary result set.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `a | b` is the union: values present in `a`, `b`, or both.
`a & b` is the intersection: values present in both sets.
`a - b` is the directional difference: values in `a` but not `b`.
`a ^ b` is the symmetric difference: values present in exactly one set.
`a <= b` checks whether `a` is a subset of `b`; `a.isdisjoint(b)` checks for no overlap.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Union, written `a | b`, returns every value present in `a`, `b`, or both. The result still contains each value once because it is a set. Use it when the question is which distinct values appear anywhere across the two groups.

Intersection, `a & b`, returns only values that belong to both sets. With `required = {'python', 'sql'}` and `known = {'python', 'git'}`, the intersection is `{'python'}`. It directly expresses a shared-membership question without a nested loop.

Difference, `a - b`, keeps values in the left set that are absent from the right. `required - known` gives missing skills, while `known - required` gives extra known skills; reversing the operands changes the question. Difference is not the same as symmetric difference.

Symmetric difference, `a ^ b`, keeps values present in exactly one input and removes the common overlap. It is different from union because union includes shared values. For the skill sets, it returns `{'sql', 'git'}`: the values on either non-overlapping side.

Use `required <= known` when the result should simply say whether every requirement is present, and `a.isdisjoint(b)` when the groups must have no overlap. Operator forms expect set-like operands, while methods such as `intersection(iterable)` accept general iterables. Non-mutating operations keep the inputs; updating variants deliberately change one set.

beats.cue: Define union as membership in either input
beats.spokenText: Union, written `a | b`, returns every value present in `a`, `b`, or both. The result still contains each value once because it is a set. Use it when the question is which distinct values appear anywhere across the two groups.

beats.spokenText: Symmetric difference, `a ^ b`, keeps values present in exactly one input and removes the common overlap. It is different from union because union includes shared values. For the skill sets, it returns `{'sql', 'git'}`: the values on either non-overlapping side.

beats.spokenText: Use `required <= known` when the result should simply say whether every requirement is present, and `a.isdisjoint(b)` when the groups must have no overlap. Operator forms expect set-like operands, while methods such as `intersection(iterable)` accept general iterables. Non-mutating operations keep the inputs; updating variants deliberately change one set.

support.title: Compare required and known skill membership
support.code:
required = {"python", "sql"}
known = {"python", "git"}

print(sorted(required | known))
print(sorted(required & known))
print(sorted(required - known))
print(sorted(required ^ known))
print(required <= known)
print(required.isdisjoint({"java"}))
support.caption: Sorting is only for stable display; each set operation is defined by membership rather than output order.

beats.recallRule: Union keeps either side, intersection keeps overlap, difference keeps left-only, and symmetric difference keeps exactly one side.

sections.title: Set algebra turns loops into named relationships
sections.content:
Each operation selects regions of two conceptual circles. Intersection selects the overlap. The two differences select opposite non-overlapping sides. Symmetric difference selects both sides but excludes the centre, while union selects every region.

Operators require set-like operands, whereas method forms such as `intersection(iterable)` can accept general iterables. Both create new sets unless an updating method such as `intersection_update` is used. Choosing a non-mutating form is safer when later code still needs the originals.

sections.title: Which region does each operation keep?
sections.content:
| Expression | Kept region | Question it answers |
|---|---|---|
| `a | b` | both sets | What appears anywhere? |
| `a & b` | overlap | What do they share? |
| `a - b` | left-only | What is missing from `b`? |
| `a ^ b` | either side, not overlap | What differs between them? |
| `a <= b` | boolean relationship | Is all of `a` contained in `b`? |

questions.question: What is the difference between `set` and `frozenset` in Python?
questions.title: Set vs Frozenset in Python
questions.direct_answer: Both `set` and `frozenset` hold distinct hashable elements and support non-mutating set operations. A `set` can add or remove elements and is unhashable; a `frozenset` cannot change after creation and is hashable when its elements are hashable, so it can itself be a dictionary key or set element.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you connect container immutability to hashability and select ordered or unordered composite keys correctly.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Describing frozenset as merely a faster set or assuming it can contain unhashable elements.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show why two frozensets with opposite construction order represent the same dictionary key.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Both types store unique hashable elements and support membership and set algebra.
A normal set cannot be a dictionary key or another set's element.
A frozenset is hashable and can represent an unordered composite key.
Use frozenset only when the group itself needs stable, value-based identity.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`set` and `frozenset` both represent unordered collections of distinct hashable elements. Both support membership checks, union, intersection, difference, and subset relationships. Neither provides a positional index or allows an unhashable list or dictionary as an element.

A normal set provides methods such as `add`, `remove`, `discard`, and `update`, so its membership can change after construction. That makes it the direct choice while collecting permissions, tracking visited nodes, or accumulating unique values. Because its value can change, the set object itself is unhashable.

A `frozenset` has no mutating methods. Once created, the membership cannot change, giving the group stable value-based identity. It is not merely a faster set, and its elements must still be hashable. Use it only when the complete unordered group should remain fixed.

A frozenset can itself be a dictionary key or an element of another set. `frozenset({'read', 'write'})` and a frozenset created in the opposite order are equal and have compatible hashes because membership, not construction order, defines the value. This works well for a cache keyed by an unordered permission group.

Choose a tuple when position and order are part of composite identity, such as `(latitude, longitude)`. Choose a frozenset when the same members in any order should represent one value. Use an ordinary set when membership is still evolving and does not itself need to be stored as a hashable key.

beats.cue: Begin with the membership behavior both types share
beats.spokenText: `set` and `frozenset` both represent unordered collections of distinct hashable elements. Both support membership checks, union, intersection, difference, and subset relationships. Neither provides a positional index or allows an unhashable list or dictionary as an element.

support.title: Same membership model, different container contract

items.label: set
items.detail: Can add, remove, and update elements; the container is unhashable.

items.label: frozenset
items.detail: Has no mutating operations and can itself participate in hash-based lookup.

beats.cue: Use set while membership is expected to evolve
beats.spokenText: A normal set provides methods such as `add`, `remove`, `discard`, and `update`, so its membership can change after construction. That makes it the direct choice while collecting permissions, tracking visited nodes, or accumulating unique values. Because its value can change, the set object itself is unhashable.

beats.cue: Use frozenset for a fixed unordered value
beats.spokenText: A `frozenset` has no mutating methods. Once created, the membership cannot change, giving the group stable value-based identity. It is not merely a faster set, and its elements must still be hashable. Use it only when the complete unordered group should remain fixed.

beats.cue: Connect fixed membership to a stable composite hash
beats.stage: A stable group can be hashed
beats.spokenText: A frozenset can itself be a dictionary key or an element of another set. `frozenset({'read', 'write'})` and a frozenset created in the opposite order are equal and have compatible hashes because membership, not construction order, defines the value. This works well for a cache keyed by an unordered permission group.

support.title: Use one unordered permission group as a key
support.code:
permissions = {"read"}
permissions.add("write")

group = frozenset(permissions)
cache = {group: "read-write policy"}

same_group = frozenset(["write", "read"])
print(cache[same_group])
print(group == same_group)
print(hash(group) == hash(same_group))
support.caption: Opposite construction order produces the same frozenset key because only membership defines equality.

beats.cue: Choose ordered or unordered composite identity
beats.spokenText: Choose a tuple when position and order are part of composite identity, such as `(latitude, longitude)`. Choose a frozenset when the same members in any order should represent one value. Use an ordinary set when membership is still evolving and does not itself need to be stored as a hashable key.
beats.recallRule: Use `set` for changing membership and `frozenset` for a fixed unordered value that may need its own hash.

sections.title: Container mutability determines whether the group has a stable hash
sections.content:
A set's membership can change, so a value-based hash could change as elements are added or removed. Storing that set as a key would make its table location unreliable. Frozenset closes the mutation operations, allowing Python to derive a stable hash from its members.

Tuple and frozenset encode different composite meanings. A tuple key preserves position and order; a frozenset key deliberately treats `{A, B}` and `{B, A}` as the same group. The domain's equality rule should choose between them.

sections.title: Same membership model, different container contract
sections.content:
| Property | `set` | `frozenset` |
|---|---:|---:|
| Unique elements | Yes | Yes |
| Add or remove after creation | Yes | No |
| Hashable container | No | Yes |
| Can be a dictionary key | No | Yes |
| Best fit | Evolving membership | Fixed unordered value |

sections.title: Use an unordered group as a cache key
sections.content:
```python
permissions = {"read"}
permissions.add("write")

group = frozenset(permissions)
cache = {group: "read-write policy"}

same_group = frozenset(["write", "read"])
print(cache[same_group])  # read-write policy
print(group == same_group)  # True
```
